classification.difficultyReason: Derive a trigonometric area model from a trapezium, solve the resulting stationary-point equation and verify the maximum in context.

content.prompt: A symmetrical gutter is made from a sheet of metal 30 cm wide by bending it twice as shown:

spec.sourceRegion: Question 30, below the parts on the left
spec.description: Open symmetrical trapezoidal gutter with equal-length ticks on the bottom and both sloping sides. Dotted verticals rise from the bottom corners to the dotted horizontal joining the upper endpoints. Each theta lies between a side and its adjacent vertical. The diagram is unshaded, with ordinary marks in black.
spec.mathematics: The bottom is 10 cm. Matching ticks and the 30 cm total sheet width establish that both sloping sides are also 10 cm. Theta is measured from the vertical.
spec.answerVisibility: All measurements, equal-length marks, guides and angle labels are permanent givens; no calculated dimensions or optimum angle are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the cross-sectional area of the gutter is given by $A=100\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)\,\mathrm{cm}^2$.

answer.worked:
The total sheet width is 30 cm and the base is 10 cm. Each equal sloping side therefore has length 10 cm. Since $\theta$ is measured from the vertical, the vertical height is $10\cos\theta$ cm and the horizontal projection of each side is $10\sin\theta$ cm.

The cross-section is a trapezium with lower base 10 cm, upper base $10+2(10\sin\theta)=10+20\sin\theta$ cm and height $10\cos\theta$ cm. Using $A=\frac12(a+b)h$:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\frac12(10+10+20\sin\theta)(10\cos\theta)\\A&=\frac12(20+20\sin\theta)(10\cos\theta)\\A&=100\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: For what value of $\theta$ does the gutter have maximum carrying capacity?

answer.worked:
Use radians, with $0\leq\theta\leq\frac\pi2$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=100\cos\theta+100\cos\theta\sin\theta\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=-100\sin\theta+100(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta).\end{aligned}$$
Using $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=100(-\sin\theta+1-2\sin^2\theta)\\\frac{dA}{d\theta}&=-100(2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1).\end{aligned}$$
For $\frac{dA}{d\theta}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\\\sin\theta&=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad\sin\theta=-1.\end{aligned}$$
There is no solution to $\sin\theta=-1$ in the domain. Thus
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\frac12\\\theta&=\frac\pi6.\end{aligned}$$
Check the maximum:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{d^2A}{d\theta^2}&=-100(4\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos\theta)\\A''\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=-150\sqrt3<0.\end{aligned}$$
This is the only interior stationary point. Also, $A(0)=100$ and $A(\frac\pi2)=0$, whereas $A(\frac\pi6)=75\sqrt3>100$. The maximum carrying capacity occurs at $\theta=\frac\pi6$ radians $(30^\circ)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the cross-sectional area for this value of $\theta$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=100\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\left(1+\frac12\right)\\A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=100\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\left(\frac32\right)\\A\left(\frac\pi6\right)&=75\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\end{aligned}$$
The cross-sectional area is $75\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm}^2$, approximately $130\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ to the nearest square centimetre.
